title: Funding extended drop-in hours at Royal City Mission
subtitle: Also: battery storage support, customer service strategy progress, and tracking of service review recommendations.
overview: Council approved a one-time City contribution of $250,850 from the Tax Rate Operating Contingency Reserve to extend drop-in service hours at Royal City Mission in downtown Guelph from January 1, 2023 {{vote:m4}}. The request came from the County of Wellington after Council's July direction. Staff said the extension is meant as a short-term response to cold weather, and the mission must report back by May 1 and September 1, 2023. Any future shelter funding requests go to the 2024-2027 multi-year budget process.

Council also supported Alectra Convergent Development LP's battery energy storage project proposal as part of the consent agenda {{vote:m2}}, with one councillor declaring a conflict of interest and not taking part. It received a progress report on the Service Simplified customer service strategy {{vote:m5}}, which included an improved online Report a Problem map and new service standards.

Council directed staff to propose a tracking and measurement plan for the priorities from the KPMG service rationalization report to the audit committee by Q2 2023, with annual progress reports to Council {{vote:m6}}. For residents, this means more public detail on whether efficiency efforts deliver better service or savings.

decisions.detail: Council approved a one-time $250,850 contribution from the Tax Rate Operating Contingency Reserve to extend drop-in hours from January 1, 2023, with progress reports due May 1 and September 1, 2023.
Council agreed to add the Royal City Mission pastor to the list of delegates so council members could ask questions directly.
Council reviewed Alectra Convergent Development LP's battery energy storage proposal and adopted a resolution of support for it.
Staff will bring a tracking and measurement plan for KPMG report priorities to the audit committee by Q2 2023 and report to Council annually on progress and outcomes.
Council received the report on implementing Guelph's customer service strategy.

debate: Several councillors called the drop-in funding a short-term 'band aid' for an urgent winter need, and said homelessness, mental health and addiction are city-wide and provincial problems, not only downtown ones.

One councillor raised concerns about using reserves outside the normal budget process and about accountability. Staff said the request was an emergency response, that the City will negotiate its own community benefit agreement with the mission, and that future funding belongs in strategic planning.
A delegate from the downtown advisory group supported the funding but said it does not address mental health and addiction needs, and described a longer-term system plan under development.

On customer service, councillors asked about accessibility, residents without internet access, and whether complaint-driven reporting could skew work away from planned maintenance. Staff said phone, in-person and online options stay, and safety-based work plans still guide repairs.

On the service review, the sponsoring councillor wanted clearer accountability, outcomes and cost-benefit information. A newer councillor asked whether this duplicates audit or strategic plan reporting, and staff said it complements them.
